beats.intro: Lesson fifteen. [[sub]]Two pure ways to organize, why neither works alone, and why the answer is a hybrid.
beats.boxes: What happened to the breakfast factory happens to every reasonably large organization. [[most]]Most middle managers run a department inside something bigger. [[link]]The black box you oversee is wired to other black boxes, the way the branches are wired to each other and to headquarters. [[look]]So let's look at how an organization made of smaller units can be put together.
beats.mission: There are two extremes. [[first]]The first is totally mission-oriented, and completely decentralized. [[regions]]Picture the breakfast network as regions, each with its own branches. [[all]]Every branch does everything for itself: finds its location and puts up its building, does its own merchandising, hires and keeps its own people, and does its own buying. [[report]]Each month it sends its financial statements to the corporate office. That is the whole tie-in.
beats.functional: At the other extreme is the totally functional organization, completely centralized. [[depts]]Here the corporate office has departments: merchandising, personnel, real estate and construction, purchasing, and finance. [[every]]Each department does its job at every branch. Merchandising does the merchandising everywhere. [[hire]]Personnel hires, fires and evaluates the staff at all the branches. And so on.
beats.pull: Each extreme has a pull. [[local]]We want each branch manager free to respond to local conditions. That pulls toward mission. [[scale]]We also want the obvious economies of scale, and to spread the expertise we have in each area across the whole company. That pulls toward function. [[comp]]So real organizations look for a compromise, and managers have searched for it for a long time. [[sloan]]Alfred Sloan, summing up decades at General Motors, said good management rests on reconciling centralization and decentralization. [[bal]]Grove puts it as a balancing act, for the best mix of responsiveness and leverage.
beats.intel: Intel itself is a hybrid. [[biz]]Its business groups are mission-oriented: components, microcomputers, and systems. [[fun]]Beside them sit the functional groups: sales, manufacturing, technology development, and administration. [[army]]Grove compares it to an army. The fighting units get blankets, paychecks, aerial surveillance and intelligence from functional groups that serve them all. [[hill]]Because no unit keeps its own support, each can concentrate on its mission, like taking a hill, with all the freedom it needs to do it.
beats.subcon: Think of the functional groups as internal subcontractors. [[sales]]Take sales. Many companies hire outside sales representatives. An internal sales group should do the same job for less, and respond faster. [[also]]Manufacturing, finance and data processing work the same way, serving all the business units. [[third]]At Intel, about two thirds of the employees worked in functional units. That shows how much they matter.
beats.pros: Why put so much in functional groups? [[econ]]First, economies of scale. Computers were very expensive. One big machine, shared by every unit, is well used. A computer for each unit would sit idle much of the time. [[shift]]Second, resources can be shifted as company priorities change. Because manufacturing is one group, the product mix can follow what the whole company needs. If each unit had its own factory, moving capacity would be slow and sticky. [[exp]]Third, specialists such as the research engineers in technology development apply their know-how across the whole company. That is enormous leverage. [[focus]]And fourth, the business units can master their own trade instead of worrying about computers, production and technology.
beats.cons: There is a price. [[over]]The biggest is information overload. A functional group must answer the demands of many different business units. [[layers]]Even stating a need gets hard: a business unit may go through several layers of management to influence a functional group's decision. [[neg]]Worst of all are the negotiations over shared, limited resources: production capacity, computer time, space in a shared building. [[fight]]Often negotiation turns into open competition between business units. [[waste]]Both waste time and energy, and neither adds to the output of the company.
beats.one: And the advantages of the mission-oriented form? [[only]]Grove says there is only one. Each unit stays in touch with the needs of its own business, and can change quickly when those needs change. That is it. Everything else favors function. [[resp]]But the business of any business is to respond to its environment. That need is so important that it always puts much of an organization into mission units. [[none]]Intel examined its organization again and again, at the top and among hundreds of middle managers. The answer was always the same: there is no alternative to the hybrid.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]The mission-oriented form gives each unit everything it needs. [[w2]]The functional form centralizes each activity for all the units. [[w3]]Function brings scale, flexibility and the leverage of expertise. [[w4]]Its price is overload, layers, and fights over shared resources. [[w5]]Mission brings one thing, responsiveness, and it is vital. So, a hybrid. Now the lesson practice.
